entities.summary:
Archermus, an Ionian master sculptor active in Chios around the mid-6th century BCE (c. 550 BCE), stands as a pivotal figure in the transition from the rigid Archaic style to the burgeoning naturalism of early Classical Greek sculpture. He is particularly renowned for his contributions to the development of winged figures, notably the 'Nike' type, and for establishing a dynastic tradition of marble carving that profoundly influenced the sculptural output of the Eastern Aegean. His workshop, which included his father Micciades and his celebrated sons Bupalus and Athenis, represented a significant artistic hub, shaping the aesthetic sensibilities and technical prowess of generations of sculptors.

Working primarily in marble, Archermus is credited with some of the earliest known representations of Nike, the goddess of victory, depicted with wings. While no works are definitively signed by Archermus himself, ancient literary sources, particularly Pliny the Elder, attribute to him and his sons a significant body of work, including a renowned statue of Nike at Delos. This statue, often associated with a fragment found on the island, is considered a crucial precursor to later, more dynamic representations of the goddess, such as those by Paionios. His innovative approach to drapery and anatomical representation helped to break away from the stiff, frontal poses characteristic of earlier Archaic kouroi and korai, infusing figures with a greater sense of movement and vitality.
